Explain in your own words what 'Enzyme Classes and Cofactor Helpers' refers to.
questions.a: Every catalyst of the cell is a protein except the few catalytic RNAs called ribozymes; the I.U.B. files them into seven reaction classes from oxidoreductases to the newer translocases, and many need helpers - organic coenzymes built from vitamins, metal ions like zinc or magnesium, or a tightly bonded prosthetic group, the naked protein being the apoenzyme and the armed pair the holoenzyme.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Enzyme Classes and Cofactor Helpers'.
questions.a: Reaction type fixes the class; vitamin-derived coenzymes and metal ions complete enzymes that cannot work alone.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Enzyme Classes and Cofactor Helpers' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Lock-Key and Induced Fit Models' refers to.
questions.a: Fischer pictured the active site in 1894 as a rigid lock pre-cut for its substrate key, while Koshland argued in 1958 that the site flexes like a glove around the hand of the substrate, aligning catalytic groups only after binding; enzymes further show group, absolute, stereo and geometrical grades of specificity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Lock-Key and Induced Fit Models'.
questions.a: Old model: rigid complementary pocket; modern model: the site reshapes around the substrate after contact.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Lock-Key and Induced Fit Models' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity' refers to.
questions.a: Reaction speed bends to the environment: heating raises activity to an optimum near body temperature then denatures the protein, each enzyme peaks at its own pH from pepsin around 1-2 to alkaline phosphatase near 10-11, and rising substrate concentration lifts the rate only until every enzyme molecule is saturated.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity'.
questions.a: Bell curves for temperature and pH, and a saturation plateau for substrate, describe every catalytic optimum.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity' taught, and from which source text?
Explain in your own words what 'Competitive and Non-Competitive Inhibition' refers to.
questions.a: Inhibitors slow catalysts either permanently, as penicillin wedging transpeptidase shut, or reversibly: look-alike inhibitors fight for the active site and only raise Km, distant-site inhibitors cripple the enzyme and only lower Vmax, and uncompetitive binders attack only the enzyme-substrate pair, moving both constants.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Competitive and Non-Competitive Inhibition'.
questions.a: Read the kinetic signature: Km up with Vmax untouched means competitive; Vmax down with Km untouched means non-competitive.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Competitive and Non-Competitive Inhibition' taught, and from which source text?
